title: Qataban
capsule: Qataban was an ancient South Arabian kingdom centred on the Baihan valley (modern Yemen) with its capital at Timna', ruled by a mukarrib (priest-king) whose title later evolved into malik (king), and whose economy rested on frankincense and myrrh trade along the overland incense routes. At its height around the third century BCE, Qataban controlled critical portions of the spice road and featured a substantial urban centre; excavations at Timna' by the American Foundation for the Study of Man in the 1950s uncovered temples, inscriptions, and evidence of sophisticated urban organization. The kingdom was progressively eroded by the rival Himyarite kingdom and Hadramawt and ceased to function as an independent polity by the late second century CE.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Archaeological work at Timna' has confirmed the capital site, but the broader territorial extent of Qataban at different periods is only partially reconstructed from inscriptions and remains contested among specialists.
